extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism; critics and writers interested in 19th-century European literature and the qualities of modern poetry/prose
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical touchstones for evaluating/producing modern (19th-century) poetry and prose, especially in relation to Goethe and Heine: originality, application of ideas, style (clarity, lightness), and the writer's relation to society and tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work from within outwards / individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist must 'work from within outwards' — only by bringing out his own individuality can he be original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement attributed to Goethe: the true poet creates from inner life rather than by external prescription. Guidance: prioritize authentic personal vision over imitating external forms or fashions. Anti-pattern: producing derivative work by adhering to external rules rather than inner feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control subject-matter and maintain objective artistic restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer should 'control his subject-matter and keep himself beautifully objective,' as the artistic school recommends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the artistic-school ideal of objectivity and measured treatment. Use it when the work requires formal distance; avoid letting passionate feeling entirely swamp the presentation when objectivity is the goal. Counterpoint in the essay: Heine sometimes rejects this strict objectivity in favour of engaged modernism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberatory function of literature / subversion of routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature should act as a 'liberator' from prescription and routine, placing the standard 'inside every man' rather than outside him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a work questions received authorities and customs and helps free readers from inherited routines. Example: Goethe's influence as a 'liberator' of poets. Scoring note: works that merely echo tradition score lower on this dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward authority — ask 'Is it so to me?'
rubrics_metrics.description: A critical stance that questions long-established truths: when told 'such a thing must be so' the proper answer is 'But is it so? Is it so to me?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the writer interrogates accepted conventions and tests them by personal/modern standards. Anti-pattern: uncritical acceptance of tradition or reliance on precedent alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply modern ideas practically (not play with ideas as toys)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas in literature should be applied to life — not treated as 'counters or marbles' — so that literature makes ideas active and practical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for work that converts intellectual energy into practical insight or influence rather than luxuriating in abstraction. Example: praise for the French tendency to apply ideas practically; criticism of German works that hoard ideas without application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of wit and seriousness (mingling wit and pathos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The effective mingling of wit and seriousness (pathos) produces characteristic and powerful prose/poetry, as in Heine's Reisebilder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how well a piece blends comic/satiric elements with genuine feeling. Examples: Heine's travel sketches where prose and verse, wit and seriousness, are mixed naturally. Anti-pattern: works in which wit undercuts sincerity or seriousness becomes humorless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, lightness, and freedom with emotional power and range
rubrics_metrics.description: Style qualities to value: clearness, lightness, and freedom united with a strong power of feeling and a wide range of subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prose/poetry for lucid expression, graceful ease, stylistic liberty, and the capacity to convey deep feeling across diverse topics. Heine is commended for this union; lack of any of these (e.g., obscurity or heaviness) counts as a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose Philistinism — resist narrowness and commonplaces
rubrics_metrics.description: A central critical aim is to attack Philistinism (Philister) — the practical narrowness, routine-mindedness, and scorn for ideas — and to champion the 'children of the light' (reformers and thinkers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether writing confronts complacency, superficial practicality, and commonplaces. Anti-pattern: complacent prose that privileges convenience or precedent over reason and ideas; examples include criticisms of English 'rule of thumb' pragmatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be a considered dissolvent of old systems (not acridly destructive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who seek to dissolve old orders must be 'dissolvents' but should avoid being 'acrid dissolvents' — i.e., destroy thoughtfully rather than venomously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tone and method in critique or revolutionary writing: effective work dismantles obsolete systems with subtlety, intelligence, and restraint rather than mere bitterness. Anti-pattern: shrill, purely destructive rhetoric that alienates potential readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesis and founding a fresh period (fusion of spirits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative originality can come from fusing different cultural/spiritual elements (e.g., French spirit + German ideas) to open a new literary period rather than merely prolonging an old one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for works that combine disparate influences into something novel and influential. Heine is praised for joining French ardour with German culture; mere continuation of an expired period is scored lower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reasoned change over appeal to precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: When reforming or suppressing what is inconvenient, appeal to reason and general principles rather than convenient precedent or forms alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate arguments and aesthetics for their appeal to rational justification vs. reliance on custom. Anti-pattern: reforms justified only by prior usage or convenience ('we did it this way'), as criticized in English practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's communicative primacy — poetry as the most effective mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is 'the most beautiful, impressive, and widely effective mode of saying things' and thus has special importance in influencing literature and society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging the impact of a work, consider how poetry's formal strengths enable it to carry ideas powerfully. This is a weighting criterion: poetic form may be given priority for societal influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being absorbed by romantic mysticism / nostalgia
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer should not be 'conquered by the Middle Age' or lose modern relevance by overindulging in mystic/romantic nostalgia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether romantic/medieval preoccupations dominate to the point that modern insight and application are sacrificed. Heine is praised for retaining modern ideas even while appreciating medieval charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained quality across collected works (few things to skip)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sign of high literary value is a collected edition 'in which there is so little to skip' — consistent quality and lack of filler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate an author's corpus for evenness of quality: frequent lapses or much skippable material reduce the author's standing. Example: Heine's collected works are cited as having very little to omit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of literature: intellectual propagation not direct politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct political action is 'not the true function of literature'; instead, literature's proper role is to propagate ideas and influence feeling and thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising politically engaged work, value its capacity to shape ideas, sentiment, and cultural practice rather than its role as a vehicle for direct political activism. Anti-pattern: judging literary success solely by political agitation or office-holding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wit and the jester-persona as political/ethical instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: The jester or satirist figure can 'bring comfort and counsel' and serve as an instrument of political and moral insight — humour may be the vehicle for serious counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the effectiveness of humorous or satiric persona in delivering critique, consolation, or moral persuasion (example: Heine as 'Conrad von der Rosen'). Poorly employed wit that only mocks without insight is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholeheartedness: avoid half-measures and condescension
rubrics_metrics.description: The true reformer/writer despises half-measures and condescension to human folly; attacks on conservatism should be made 'in the name of the idea' not ignobly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value writing that commits fully to principle and attacks conservatism with integrity and idea-driven passion. Anti-pattern: opportunistic or performative attacks lacking principled purpose (labelled 'Philistine' behaviour).

rubrics_metrics.name: National intellectual climate as enabling factor
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation's accessibility to and application of ideas (its 'intellectual life') materially supports or impedes the greatness of its writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating writers historically, consider the extent to which national receptivity to ideas enabled their success (e.g., England's Philistinism vs. Germany's wealth of ideas). This is a contextual criterion rather than a stylistic one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage and creative activity under suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal fortitude — continuing to compose with 'undiminished fire' amid suffering — is an attribute that figures in critical judgement of a writer's moral and artistic stature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider biographical resilience as a contributing, though not decisive, factor in appraising a writer's greatness (example: Heine's productivity despite paralytic illness). Avoid conflating suffering with automatic artistic merit.
